compare-4x8-vs-5x5.html.text:
CUT LIST OPTIMIZER

4×8 vs 5×5: buy the size that costs less, not the one that sounds cheaper.

Baltic birch 5×5 sheets nest some cabinet work onto one square. Construction 4×8 is cheaper per sheet and takes long parts a 60-inch square cannot. Paste the parts, type what your yard charges, and see which size you should actually load.

Open the full sheet-goods layout tool if you also need the cutting diagram.

Worked example: four 28-inch doors

Four 28 × 28 doors, 1/8-inch kerf, no edge trim. That is a real cabinet door blank, not a toy list.

  • 5×5 at $90: one sheet, $90. High utilization, one trip.
  • 4×8 at $42: two sheets, $84. Six dollars less cash, more offcut.
  • 4×4 at $22: four sheets, $88. Easy to carry, not the cheap buy.

Flip the 5×5 to $55 and the 4×8 to $62 and the ranking reverses: one Baltic sheet is $69 cheaper than two 4×8s. The answer is the yard ticket, not the folklore.

Rank this list on your prices

Change a price or the parts to rerank.

When 4×8 is the only size that works

A 72-inch bookcase side will not fit a 5×5 even rotated. The 5×5 can be cheaper per sheet and still be the wrong buy because two pieces never leave the oversize list. Long casework, stair treads, and tall doors are 4×8 (or 5×10) jobs.

Common questions

Is 5×5 Baltic birch cheaper than 4×8 for cabinet doors?

Only if the extra you pay per sheet is less than the sheets you avoid. Four 28-inch doors fit on one 5×5 and need two 4×8s. At $90 versus $42, the two 4×8 sheets still cost $6 less. At $55 versus $62, the single 5×5 wins by $69.

When does a 4×8 beat a 5×5 even if I need more sheets?

When the 4×8 is cheap enough that two (or three) of them still cost less than one Baltic sheet, or when a long part will not fit the 60-inch square at all — a 72-inch bookcase side is the usual case.

Should I buy half-sheets instead?

Half-sheets (4×4) are easy to carry and sometimes cheaper per sheet, but you often buy more of them and pay for more edge trim and kerf. Rank them on the same list before you assume they save money.

No warranty. This free tool is provided as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering, financial, or business advice and does not replace a qualified professional. The ranking is a heuristic packing of your list — it is not a supplier quote. Review and verify prices, dimensions, and the plan before you buy or cut. FOR WOODWORKERS, SIGN SHOPS, AND MAKERS

Buy less stock. Cut with a plan.

Paste the pieces you need. Get a sheet-by-sheet layout for plywood, MDF, or acrylic, or a bar-by-bar plan for linear stock — with your saw kerf accounted for and the offcut shown before you buy. Which board length should you buy?

Same cuts, the lengths a yard sells. Ranked by purchased length, so an 8 ft stick wins over a 12 ft stick when both cover the list with one bar.

Enter required cuts to compare common stock lengths.

Common questions

How does the sheet layout decide where each piece goes?

Largest pieces are placed first, into the first spot on the sheet they fit, with your saw kerf and edge trim already subtracted from the usable area. It is a fast, practical heuristic, not a proven-optimal packing — always confirm the diagram against your own stock and saw before cutting.

What does adding grain to the end of a line do?

It locks that one piece to its listed orientation even when "Pieces may be rotated 90°" is checked for everything else. Use it for a veneer face, a printed panel, or anything where the direction has to run one way — leaving rotation on for the rest of the list still lets the layout use less material on parts that don't care which way they're cut.

What's the difference between "material used" and "offcut area"?

Material used is the actual area of the parts you listed; offcut area is everything left over on the sheets you buy, including the strips lost to kerf and edge trim. Utilization is used area divided by total sheet area bought — on the default three-part list it lands well under 100%, because a sheet you buy is a fixed size whether or not the parts fill it.

When should I use the sheet-size or board-length comparison instead of just my usual size?

Whenever more than one size is actually stocked at the yard. The comparison re-runs the same cut list against each candidate size — for example a 4×8 against a 5×5 or a half-sheet — and ranks them by sheets needed, or by total cost once you enter a price for each. A size that looks cheaper per sheet can still lose if it takes more sheets to fit the same parts.

Does the planner use my on-hand offcuts before buying new stock?

Yes, on both tabs. Cuts and panels are placed into your listed offcuts first, and only the pieces that don't fit any offcut count toward new stock to purchase. On the sheet-goods tab an offcut is sized as width x height and can be larger than the sheet you'd otherwise buy — a leftover full sheet, say. On both tabs an untouched offcut stays off the plan entirely, since it's still on the rack, not consumed. On the default examples, the on-hand list already covers part of the required list, which is why "Sheets to buy" or "New pieces to buy" can come in lower than the raw part count would suggest.

Is my cut list uploaded anywhere?

No. The layout, comparisons, and printable plan are all computed in your browser. An optional saved draft and anonymous local usage counts stay on this device only — both can be turned off and cleared with the checkbox and button below.

Weighing this against a hosted optimizer? See this cut list optimizer vs. optiCutter and CutList Optimizer. Curious how much planning by hand actually costs? See this optimizer vs. planning cuts by hand.

Pricing a different kind of print run instead of sheet goods? See the 3D Print Price Calculator, which prices a print from filament, electricity, and printer wear the same way this tool prices a cutting plan from sheet and board cost.

Drafts are saved only on this device.

vs-opticutter-and-cutlist-optimizer.html.text:
← Cut List Optimizer

This cut list optimizer vs. optiCutter and CutList Optimizer

All three nest parts onto sheets and respect kerf and grain. The differences worth knowing are where the cutting runs, whether there is a plan tier above you, and whether the offcuts already on your rack count.

What each tool is

optiCutter and CutList Optimizer are hosted cutting-optimization services. You enter stock and parts in a web app, their servers compute the nesting, and you get cutting diagrams back. Both publish a free tier alongside paid plans, and both are established tools with real users — a woodworker or sign shop that wants saved project libraries, material catalogues, an API, or a vendor with a support desk is better served by one of them than by this page, and that is a genuine reason to pay for software.

This calculator is a single static page. The nesting runs in your own browser, in JavaScript, on the page you have already loaded. There is no account, no sign-in, no per-day calculation count, and no tier above you that a big enough job pushes you into — not as a promotion, but because there is no server doing the work and therefore nothing to meter. Nothing you type is uploaded, and once the page has loaded it keeps cutting with the connection off, which matters more in a shop with bad Wi-Fi than it sounds on a spec sheet.

No prices or tier limits are quoted for either service on this page, on purpose. Their plans and limits are theirs to change, the third-party round-ups that publish figures for them disagree with each other, and neither vendor's own site is reachable from the environment this page was written in. Rather than repeat a number we could not check, we link to their pages: read the current terms there.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Lay out a one-off cabinet or sign job on sheet goods, with kerf and grain direction handled. Any of the three. This one if you would rather not create an account for a single job.
Use the offcuts already stacked against the shop wall before buying a new sheet. This calculator — type them into the on-hand box and they are placed first, and the plan tells you how many new sheets that avoided.
Decide whether to buy 4×8 or 5×5 stock for this cut list, on cash rather than on offcut area. This calculator's 4×8 vs 5×5 sheet comparison.
Rank 8 ft, 10 ft, 12 ft and 16 ft boards for a linear cut list before a lumber run. This calculator — the board-length comparison is on the same page as the linear plan.
Keep a library of saved projects, a material catalogue with costs, or edge-banding calculations. A hosted service. This page keeps one working draft in your own browser and has no catalogue and no edge-banding model.
Call an optimizer from your own software. A hosted service with an API. This tool has none.
Run a big list without wondering whether it counts against a plan. This calculator — there is no plan to count against.
Work in a shop with no reliable connection. This calculator — it keeps working after the page has loaded.

Most shops are well served by both shapes: a hosted service when the job is a recurring product line with a material catalogue behind it, and a page like this one when you are standing at the rack with a list and want a plan before you cut.

What this tool actually does

Verifiable from the page itself rather than from a feature grid:

  • Sheet nesting with saw kerf and edge trim taken out of usable area, and a drawn layout per sheet.
  • Grain lock per part, so a face-grain piece is not quietly rotated to make the nesting look better.
  • On-hand offcuts placed before any new sheet is counted as bought, with the sheets avoided reported.
  • Sheet-size comparison — the same cut list costed across 4×8, 5×5 and 4×4 at your prices, because the cheaper sheet is not always the cheaper buy.
  • Board-length comparison for linear cuts, ranking common stock lengths on the same list.
  • A printable job ticket and a copy-to-clipboard plan for both the sheet and linear modes.
  • A draft kept in your own browser, so a reload does not lose the list you typed.

And what it does not do, stated plainly: no accounts, no saved project library beyond that single draft, no material or price catalogue, no edge-banding model, no API, and no support desk. Those are the things a paid service is for.

Open the Cut List Optimizer to put your own list through it.

Common questions

Should I use this cut list optimizer or optiCutter or CutList Optimizer?

All three nest rectangular parts onto sheet stock and account for saw kerf and grain direction, so for a one-off panel layout any of them will give you a workable cutting diagram. The difference is the shape of the product. optiCutter and CutList Optimizer are hosted services: the optimization runs on their servers, and each publishes a free tier alongside paid plans, so a large enough job or a heavy enough week can put you above the free line. This calculator is a static page — the nesting runs in your own browser, there is no account, no plan above you, and no size at which it asks for money. It also does something neither of them is built around: you can type in the offcuts already on your rack, and it will place parts on those before it counts a new sheet as bought. If you want saved project libraries, material catalogues, an API, or a vendor with a support desk, a hosted service is the right shape and this page is not trying to talk you out of one.

Does this cut list optimizer have a free-tier limit?

No. There is no account, no sign-in, no per-day calculation count and no paid tier, because there is no server doing the work — the layout is computed by JavaScript on the page you have already loaded. The practical ceiling is your own device: a cut list of a few hundred parts lays out in well under a second on a phone. Nothing you type is uploaded, and once the page has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Is this page affiliated with optiCutter or CutList Optimizer?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by optiCutter or CutList Optimizer, and the names are used here only to describe what this tool is and is not. Their plans and limits are theirs to change, so this page deliberately quotes no price and no tier limit for either — check their own pages for current terms.

vs-planning-cuts-by-hand.html.text:
← Cut List Optimizer

Cut list optimizer vs. planning cuts by hand

Cutting a job list top to bottom, one part type at a time, gets every individual length right. What it doesn't do is hold a cut back from an early part type to pair it with a complementary length from a later one -- and that pairing, not the arithmetic on any one cut, is what decides how many boards the job actually needs.

What a hand plan gets right, and what it doesn't

Planning by hand, part type by part typeThis optimizer
Each cut's own lengthCorrect, if measured carefullyCorrect, from the same list
Pairing across part typesNot considered -- a board closed out while cutting one part is not reopened for a later partHolds every board open until nothing left in the list fits it
Boards kept in progress at onceEffectively one -- finish a part, close its boards, move onAs many as the list needs, tracked automatically
Offcuts already on the rackA separate mental note, easy to forget mid-jobPlaced into before any new board counts as bought

Same 24 parts, two plans

Take a face-frame job: 6 stiles at 22", 8 rails at 34", 6 aprons at 46", and 4 legs at 58", cut from 8-foot (96") stock with a 1/8" kerf at $42 a board. Cutting the ticket the way it's usually written -- all 6 stiles first, then all 8 rails, then the aprons, then the legs -- books:

Boards booked13
Utilization73.1%
Waste (length not cut, net of kerf)334.63"
Cost at $42/board$546.00

The same 24 parts, planned by holding every board open until nothing left in the list fits it, book onto 10 boards: three rail-and-leg pairs (58"+34"), three rail pairs with an apron (46"+46"), a rail-stile-apron mix (46"+34"), two stile-and-rail combinations (34"+34"+22"), and one board of stiles alone (22"x4):

Boards booked10
Utilization95.0%
Waste (length not cut, net of kerf)46.25"
Cost at $42/board$420.00

Three fewer boards, $126 not spent, on a list where every measurement was correct either way. The difference is entirely which board each cut lands on -- specifically, that a 58" leg and a 34" rail (92" together) share a 96" board with only the kerf between them, a pairing a part-by-part read-through never has reason to try because the rails haven't come up yet when the legs are being cut.

Why the gap grows with the list, not the mistakes on it

Nothing about the hand plan above was careless -- every cut was measured and placed correctly onto a board that fit it. The gap comes from having only one part type open on the saw at a time, so a board with room left over when a part type finishes is closed out rather than held for a length that hasn't come up yet. A longer, more varied list gives this more chances to happen, not fewer: the more distinct lengths a job has, the more complementary pairs exist to miss by cutting in ticket order.

Open the Cut List Optimizer to plan your own list against the boards or offcuts you actually have. Comparing sheet sizes instead of board lengths? See 4×8 vs 5×5 sheets. Weighing this against a hosted optimizer? See this cut list optimizer vs. optiCutter and CutList Optimizer.

Common questions

What does planning cuts by hand usually get right, and what does it miss?

Cutting a job list top to bottom, one part type at a time, gets every individual cut right -- the lengths are correct and nothing is wasted through error. What it doesn't do is hold a cut back from one part type to pair it with a complementary length from a different part type later in the list, because by the time that later, shorter part comes up, the board it could have shared has usually already been closed out and set aside. That pairing is exactly what determines how many boards the job actually needs.

Why does cutting by part type use more boards than the same list needs?

Because a job ticket is naturally grouped by part -- all the stiles, then all the rails, then the aprons, then the legs -- and a board closed out while cutting stiles is not reopened once rails come up, even if a rail would have fit in the space left over. Holding it open across part types means keeping several boards in progress on the saw at once, which is exactly the bookkeeping a hand plan skips in favor of finishing one part before starting the next.

How big is the gap in practice?

On a 24-part face-frame list -- 6 stiles at 22 in, 8 rails at 34 in, 6 aprons at 46 in, 4 legs at 58 in, cut from 96 in stock with a 1/8 in kerf -- cutting each part type in order books 13 boards at 73.1% utilization. This optimizer's plan for the identical list books 10 boards at 95.0% utilization: 3 fewer boards, worth $126 at $42 a board, entirely from which board a cut lands on, with no part mismeasured either way.

Does this optimizer know my local lumber prices?

No. It has no data on what your yard charges. It takes your cut list, your stock length, your kerf, and the price you enter for a board, and turns that into a plan and a cost -- the packing arithmetic a hand plan skips, not a price lookup.
